Capacitors & Tone Controls / Technical reference

How a Guitar Tone Control Works

Understand the capacitor and potentiometer as a frequency-dependent loading branch toward ground, not an inline filter in the main signal path.

Published 4 October 2026

In this guide
  1. Start with the branch
  2. Why capacitance makes the loading frequency-dependent
  3. What the tone pot changes
  4. Choose values as a network
  5. Separate specification from mythology
  6. Understand, compare, then wire
  7. Next steps

Start with the branch

In a conventional passive tone circuit, the capacitor and the tone pot provide a path from a signal node toward ground. The main signal route still runs from the selected pickup to the volume input, through the wiper and to the output jack TIP. The tone network loads that signal; it is not simply a capacitor placed inline between pickup and output.

For the simple Modern arrangement described here, the branch originates at the volume signal-input lug 3. Other supported wiring arrangements can move that connection and change interactions. Use the diagram for the actual configuration rather than transferring a generic picture to every guitar. Volume lug 1 is ground, not the signal-input attachment for this branch.

Why capacitance makes the loading frequency-dependent

A capacitor’s impedance changes with frequency. For an ideal capacitor, the magnitude of capacitive reactance is |Xc| = 1 / (2πfC). At a higher frequency, the same capacitor presents less reactance; at a higher capacitance, it presents less reactance at the same frequency. That is why this branch affects the electrical response differently across the spectrum.

The equation describes the capacitor, not the whole guitar. The pickup’s impedance, tone resistance, volume control and external load also contribute. A passive pickup has inductance, so this is not accurately reduced to an isolated single-pole RC filter with a universal cut-off frequency. A resonance and its damping can change as the controls move.

What the tone pot changes

The tone pot changes the resistance associated with the capacitor’s path to ground. At the setting commonly called tone up, a large resistance limits the branch’s loading, but an ordinary pot still leaves a finite network connected. At tone down, the resistance is reduced and the capacitor has a stronger effect on the response. The physical direction depends on how the terminals are connected.

This is why the useful knob range depends on taper as well as the capacitor. A no-load tone control, where specified, disconnects at a particular end setting and should not be assumed equivalent to an ordinary pot. Check the actual part and circuit if you are comparing the fully open position.

Choose values as a network

Tone-network decisions
VariableWhy it matters
CapacitanceChanges frequency-dependent branch impedance
Tone resistance and taperChanges loading and its progression with rotation
Pickup/source impedanceChanges the interaction and resonance
Volume and cable loadChanges the surrounding network

Common 0.022 µF and 0.047 µF choices are useful starting points, not single-coil or humbucker laws. At the same low tone resistance, the larger capacitor generally shifts the heavily affected region toward lower frequencies. At a more resistive tone setting, differences can be smaller and remain dependent on the rest of the circuit.

Separate specification from mythology

Measured capacitance, tolerance, leakage where relevant, physical dimensions and reliable construction are useful specifications. The material name by itself does not establish an audible advantage. Two equivalent components used within their ratings obey the same circuit relationships; any claimed difference needs a controlled comparison and an identified electrical cause.

A capacitor voltage rating is a permitted operating limit, not a tone-intensity setting. A passive guitar normally produces small signals, but the replacement still needs a suitable rating and sound insulation. Avoid exposed leads that can contact grounded metal or a neighbouring terminal.

Understand, compare, then wire

Identify the signal node and ground return in the wiring reference before soldering. Keep the jack TIP and sleeve identities distinct. Inspect for solder bridges and unintended shorts after assembly. A tone control that mutes the entire guitar may have a wiring fault; do not assume that the capacitor value alone explains a total loss of output.

A model has boundaries

Signal Forge provides an electrical comparison for supported assumptions and configurations. Read those limits. It does not predict the amplifier, speaker, acoustic level or a player’s preference.

For a useful experiment, hold the pickup, cable and volume constant, then compare capacitance and tone positions. Document the settings so the comparison is repeatable. The aim is to understand an adjustment, not to find a universally correct capacitor.
